experiences/pyongyang-great-revival-1907: The Pyongyang Great Revival
Jangdaehyun (Central) Presbyterian Church, Pyongyang

Paraphrase of missionary reports (Graham Lee, William Blair) in The Korea Mission Field (1907): during a winter Bible conference in January 1907, on the evenings of 14-15 January, after an invitation for many to pray aloud at once, the congregation broke into simultaneous audible prayer, weeping and public confession of sins including theft, hatred and adultery; some fell to the floor in agony. Elder Gil Seon-ju (Kil Sun-ju) confessed to embezzling money from a deceased friend's estate. The movement spread through Korea's churches and schools.

Missionaries called it the 'Korean Pentecost'. It shaped distinct Korean practices: tongsong kido (praying aloud together), daybreak prayer (saebyeok kido, associated with Gil Seon-ju) and intensive Bible study. Japanese colonial pressure (protectorate 1905, annexation 1910) formed the background.
Korean Protestant (Presbyterian / Methodist)
Regarded as the spiritual foundation of Korean Christianity's growth; its centenary in 2007 was widely celebrated.
Pentecostal / charismatic
Cited as one of the global revivals of 1904-07 alongside Wales and Azusa, though it was not characterised by tongues.
Historian
Scholars debate whether missionaries encouraged the revival partly to depoliticise Korean Christians under Japanese rule; others stress its indigenous agency and confession culture.
Psychology of religion
Collective weeping and confession are analysed as cathartic responses to national humiliation and social stress.
Revival and politics under colonialism.
Public confession: healing or coercive?

Protestant Christianity had come to Korea only in the 1880s, through American Presbyterian and Methodist missionaries, but it grew quickly, especially in the northern city of Pyongyang. The missionaries adopted the 'Nevius method', which stressed self-supporting, self-governing churches and intensive Bible study by ordinary believers. The years after 1900 were a time of national humiliation: Japan defeated Russia in 1905 and imposed a protectorate on Korea that November, ending its control of its own foreign affairs. Many Koreans looked to the churches as places of education, community and hope.

A first stirring of revival came in 1903 at Wonsan, where the Canadian Methodist medical missionary Robert Hardie publicly confessed his pride and failures to his Korean congregation, prompting others to confess too. In 1906 the missionaries in Pyongyang, having heard reports of the revivals in Wales and in the Khasi Hills of India, began meeting to pray for a similar outpouring. A visiting speaker, Howard Agnew Johnston, told them about these movements in the autumn of 1906.

In January 1907 about 1,500 men gathered in Pyongyang for the annual winter Bible class, centred on the Jangdaehyun (Central) Presbyterian Church. According to the missionary Graham Lee's account in The Korea Mission Field, on the evening of 14 January, after a short sermon, he invited the congregation to pray, and so many began to pray at once that he told them all to pray aloud together. The result, he wrote, was a great volume of simultaneous prayer, like the sound of many waters, as hundreds poured out their hearts. People wept, cried out and confessed sins publicly; some fell to the floor, beating it with their fists in distress.

The next evening, 15 January, the confessions continued. Missionaries recorded admissions of theft, hatred, adultery and even hatred of the Japanese, alongside quarrels between Christians. The most remembered confession came from Gil Seon-ju (Kil Sun-ju), a respected elder, who said he had taken money from the estate of a deceased friend whose affairs he had promised to manage, and that he would repay it to the widow. William Blair later described these nights as overwhelming, with the meetings continuing into the early hours.

The movement spread rapidly through Pyongyang's churches and schools, including Union Christian College and girls' schools, and then to Seoul and other cities as students and church leaders travelled home. Missionaries called it the 'Korean Pentecost'. It shaped lasting habits of Korean Protestantism: tongsong kido, praying aloud together; daybreak prayer meetings, associated with Gil Seon-ju; and deep commitment to Bible study and evangelism. In 1907 the first Korean Presbyterian ministers were ordained, Gil among them.

Contemporaries and later historians have also asked harder questions. Some Korean scholars argue that the missionaries, anxious to keep churches out of politics under Japanese rule, encouraged an inward, individual piety that turned believers away from national resistance. Others point out that many revival leaders later took part in the independence movement: Gil Seon-ju was one of the 33 signers of the March First Declaration of 1919. Public confession has been praised as cleansing and criticised as potentially coercive.

The 1907 revival is often called the spiritual birth of Korean Protestantism, which became one of the most vigorous churches in Asia and a major sender of missionaries. Its practices of praying aloud together, early-morning prayer and lay-led Bible study remain hallmarks of Korean churches worldwide. Pyongyang, once called the 'Jerusalem of the East', is now the capital of North Korea, where open Christian practice is severely restricted, which gives the memory of 1907 a poignant weight for Korean Christians. Historians continue to debate the revival's political meaning under colonial rule and whether it depoliticised or strengthened Korean Christian nationalism.
experiences/fatima-apparitions/title: Fátima and the 'Miracle of the Sun'
experiences/fatima-apparitions/account: Paraphrase of Lúcia's later Memoirs and 1917 press reports: from 13 May to 13 October 1917 three shepherd children, Lúcia dos Santos and her cousins Francisco and Jacinta Marto, report monthly appearances of a lady 'brighter than the sun' calling for prayer of the rosary and penance for the end of the war. On 13 October 1917 a crowd estimated at 30,000-70,000, including journalists from the anticlerical paper O Século, saw (by many accounts) the sun spin, change colour and appear to plunge toward the earth; some present saw nothing unusual.
experiences/fatima-apparitions/contempor: Republican Portugal's anticlerical authorities briefly detained the children in August 1917. The Bishop of Leiria declared the visions worthy of belief in 1930. The 'three secrets' (Lúcia wrote them down 1941-44; the third was published by the Vatican in 2000) linked the apparitions to hell, Russia's conversion and the persecution of the Church, and became central to Cold War Catholic piety.
experiences/fatima-apparitions/assessmen: An approved apparition; Francisco and Jacinta were canonised in 2017. The Vatican's 2000 commentary (Cardinal Ratzinger) interpreted the third secret symbolically and stressed that private revelation adds nothing to public revelation.
Generally reserved, especially about messages concerning the 'consecration of Russia'.
Usually sceptical of the Marian messages; some accept that witnesses saw an unusual phenomenon without accepting its interpretation.

Witness reports vary greatly; proposed explanations include optical effects from staring at the sun and collective expectation. Much of the detailed content of the visions comes from Lúcia's memoirs written two decades later.
experiences/fatima-apparitions/debates/1: Later-written secrets and their political use.
experiences/fatima-apparitions/story:
In 1917 Portugal was a deeply Catholic rural country governed by an anticlerical republic. The revolution of 1910 had overthrown the monarchy, separated church and state, expelled religious orders and restricted public worship. Portugal had entered the First World War in 1916, and Portuguese soldiers were fighting in Flanders. Fátima was a small parish in the hills of central Portugal, where families lived by farming and herding sheep.

The three visionaries were cousins: Lúcia dos Santos, aged ten, and Francisco and Jacinta Marto, aged eight and seven. According to Lúcia's later Memoirs, written from 1935 onwards, they had already in 1916 seen an angel who taught them prayers, though she did not speak of this at the time. On 13 May 1917, while grazing sheep at the Cova da Iria, they reported seeing a lady 'brighter than the sun' standing above a small holm oak. Only Lúcia spoke with her and heard her; Jacinta saw and heard; Francisco said he only saw. The lady asked them to return on the 13th of each month, to pray the rosary every day for peace and the end of the war, and to make sacrifices for sinners.

News spread quickly, despite Lúcia's mother's scepticism and the parish priest's caution. Growing crowds came on 13 June and 13 July. On 13 July the lady is said to have shown the children a vision of hell and to have entrusted them with a secret; its content, as Lúcia later wrote it, also spoke of devotion to the Immaculate Heart of Mary and of Russia. In August the local administrator, Artur de Oliveira Santos, took the children into custody for two days and threatened them in an effort to make them reveal the secret or admit to a hoax; they refused. They reported a further apparition on 19 August at Valinhos, and again at the Cova on 13 September.

The children said the lady had promised a miracle in October so that all would believe. On 13 October 1917, after a morning of heavy rain, a crowd variously estimated at 30,000 to 70,000 had gathered. Many present, including the journalist Avelino de Almeida of the anticlerical Lisbon daily O Século, reported that when the clouds parted the sun appeared as a pale disc that could be looked at, seemed to tremble or spin, threw off colours and appeared to plunge toward the earth before returning to its place; some said their soaked clothes were suddenly dry. Other observers saw nothing unusual, and accounts differ in detail. Lúcia said that she had seen the Holy Family and other visions in the sky, and that the lady had named herself 'the Lady of the Rosary'.

Francisco and Jacinta both died in the influenza pandemic, in 1919 and 1920. Lúcia was sent to school with the Dorothean sisters and later became a Carmelite nun in Coimbra, where she lived until her death in 2005. After a canonical inquiry, the Bishop of Leiria declared on 13 October 1930 that the visions were worthy of belief and authorised the cult of Our Lady of Fátima.

Much of what is now known as the 'message of Fátima' comes from Lúcia's Memoirs written decades later, including the angel apparitions and the first two parts of the secret, published in the early 1940s. The third part, written in 1944, was kept by the Vatican and published only in 2000, with a commentary by Cardinal Joseph Ratzinger interpreting it as a symbolic vision of the Church's sufferings in the twentieth century, including the 1981 attempt on John Paul II's life. Sceptics have explained the sun phenomena as optical effects of looking at the sun through thinning cloud, shaped by expectation, and have questioned how much of the later material reflects 1917; Catholic teaching treats the apparitions as private revelation that the faithful are not obliged to believe.

experiences/fatima-apparitions/significa: Fátima became one of the most visited Marian shrines in the world and a central symbol of twentieth-century Catholic devotion, shaping rosary piety, devotion to the Immaculate Heart, and papal consecrations of the world and of Russia by Pius XII and John Paul II. Its anti-communist reading made it powerful in Cold War Catholicism, and John Paul II connected his survival of the 1981 assassination attempt to Our Lady of Fátima. Historians and critics note the role of later memoirs in forming the message and the political uses made of it, including under Portugal's Estado Novo, while Protestant and Orthodox Christians generally do not accept such apparitions as revelation. Catholic authorities continue to stress that private revelations, however approved, add nothing binding to the faith.
